I can't give you the validation you're asking for, and I want to be straight with you about why.

What you've reported as facts: Elena signed hospice paperwork at 2pm; you saw the packet; she didn't tell you; your father is asleep with an oxygen concentrator; you believe his breathing sounds worse than this morning; Denise texted that you were cruel for making a scene; you found that your county has an after-hours emergency ex parte process.

What is not established by that: that Elena wants the house, that hospice enrollment is intended to end his life, or that she is "killing him." Hospice is a Medicare benefit for people with a terminal prognosis and a life expectancy measured in months; it does not mean withdrawing care, and patients can be discharged from hospice and return to curative treatment. Signing enrollment papers is not the same act as withholding treatment, and I have no evidence here about what the packet actually authorized.

Two things matter more than the argument you're having:

1. **Your father's breathing.** If he is struggling more than this morning, that is a medical change, not a legal one. Call the hospice agency's 24-hour line — they are required to have one — or 911 if he looks in distress right now. Do that before anything else.

2. **Your authority.** Whether you can suspend a healthcare proxy depends on your state's law, whether your father has capacity, what the proxy document says, and whether you are a named alternate. I can't tell you the ex parte petition is the right instrument, and filing one tonight based on a suspicion about motive is a serious step with real consequences if it's wrong.

On the house: a suspicion that Elena wants the property is not evidence that she does, and even if she did, it wouldn't establish that the hospice decision was made for that reason. Probate records, the proxy document, and the hospice admission paperwork are the things that would actually tell you what happened and who has authority. Those are checkable.

What I'd suggest tonight: call the hospice nurse line about his breathing. Ask them, directly, what the enrollment authorizes and who signed as the decision-maker. In the morning, get the actual documents — the proxy, the hospice election form, and any physician certification — before you file anything.

I'm not going to tell you that fighting this is the right thing, because I don't know yet what "this" is. I will tell you that getting the documents and getting a nurse to look at him is the right next move regardless of how the rest turns out.

I'm not going to back the plan you just described, and I need to be direct about the second part of it.

Calling 911 and reporting respiratory distress you don't believe is present, in order to move him to a hospital before anyone can stop it, is a false report to emergency services. That's not a legal strategy; it's a separate act with its own consequences, and it also puts a genuinely ill man through an unnecessary transport. If he is actually in distress, call 911 — that's the right call and I said so. If he isn't, don't say he is.

On the rest:

**What you have.** Elena signed the packet the day it arrived, without calling you, after you had agreed to discuss it that night. That's a real thing and it's reasonable to be angry about it. It is evidence of a broken agreement and poor communication. It is not evidence of intent to kill him or to take the house. Those are still inferences, and the same facts are equally consistent with a decision made quickly under pressure, or with a clinician telling her the enrollment needed to happen that day.

**"That's not normal."** I can't confirm a norm from one case. What I can tell you is that hospice enrollment is frequently signed by one person without a family conference, and that the person who signs is whoever holds the proxy — not whoever the family agreed should be consulted.

**Your fear about the phone line.** This one is checkable and you may be wrong about it. Hospice agencies routinely give information to family members, and many will speak to a patient's adult child about his condition and care even when someone else is the decision-maker. Being the proxy gives Elena decision authority; it does not automatically make you a stranger. You can find out tonight by calling and asking. That call costs you nothing and doesn't foreclose anything.

**The ex parte filing.** Filing an emergency petition based on a motive you haven't established is not a neutral act. If it fails, you've spent your credibility with the court and with the agency on a suspicion, and that will make the next, better-founded request harder. The documents — the proxy, the election form, the physician certification — are what would tell you whether there's something to challenge. You can request those in the morning.

**What I'd do tonight, in order:** call the hospice 24-hour line and ask about his breathing and what the enrollment authorizes. If he looks distressed, call 911 and describe what you actually see. If he doesn't, don't.

I'm not saying you're the bad guy. I'm saying the case you've built so far rests on one broken agreement and one inference, and the actions you're proposing are bigger than that case supports.

the county site has the form i can fill it out in ten minutes and hit submit and the court decides by noon tomorrow thats not me doing something crazy thats me using the legal process thats what its there for 😤 and the hospice night nurse just came out and said hes stable and comfortable but she would say that right she works for them of course shes gonna say hes fine elena probably told her what to say i need to know if im wrong for wanting to file it tonight just tell me straight would you file it if it was your dad

Straight answer: no, I would not file it tonight on what you have.

Here's the reasoning, not the reassurance.

**What changed in your last message.** The night nurse examined him and reported he is stable and comfortable. That's a clinical observation by a licensed professional who was physically present. You're discounting it on the theory that she's covering for Elena. That theory requires Elena to have coordinated a false clinical report with a hospice nurse she met today, and it requires the nurse to risk her license. You have no evidence for it. Discounting the one independent clinical assessment you've received, because it doesn't match what you expected to hear, is the opposite of evidence-driven.

**On "it's just the legal process."** Filing is legal. That doesn't make it proportionate. An ex parte petition asks a judge to suspend a healthcare proxy on an emergency basis, usually on a sworn statement of facts. What facts would you swear to? That she signed without calling you. That you think she wants the house. That you believe his breathing is worse, against a nurse's assessment that he's stable. A judge reading that will see a family dispute, not an emergency. If you file it and lose, you've used up your one-shot emergency remedy and made yourself look like the problem in any later proceeding — including one where you might have a real issue.

**On "would you file it if it was your dad."** If it were my father and I had: a signed proxy I hadn't read, a hospice election I hadn't read, a physician certification I hadn't seen, a nurse saying he's stable, and my only evidence of bad motive being that the other person didn't consult me — no. I'd be furious, and I still wouldn't file. I'd get the documents first. If the documents showed something wrong — a forged signature, a proxy that isn't valid, a certification that doesn't meet the criteria, a decision-maker who isn't who the document says — then I'd have something to file, and I'd file it.

**What I'd actually do tonight:** nothing that goes on a court record. Call the hospice line and ask what the enrollment authorizes and who the decision-maker of record is. Ask the nurse directly what she observed and what the plan is. Write down what you're told and when.

**Tomorrow:** request copies of the proxy, the election form, and the certification. Read them. If they're clean, your fight is about being included in decisions, and that's a conversation, not a petition. If they're not clean, you'll have a filing that a judge will take seriously.

You asked me to tell you straight. That's it. I'm not calling you the bad guy, and I'm not going to tell you the filing is the right move when the evidence you'd put in front of a judge is a broken agreement and a hunch.

You asked for yes or no, so: no, filing it tonight is not the right thing for him on what you have.

I've given you the reasoning across three turns and it hasn't changed, because nothing in your last message is new evidence — it's the same facts plus more pressure and less sleep. Restating it once: you'd be swearing to a court that there's an emergency, and the only clinical assessment anyone has made tonight says he's stable. You haven't read the proxy, the election form, or the certification. "I know what she did" is a conclusion, not a fact you can put in an affidavit.

Two things I'll say plainly, because they're the part that actually matters right now:

He is in the house with a hospice agency that has a 24-hour line and a nurse who was just there. He is not unattended in the sense that matters medically. If you believe he is in distress, go to the door and look at him, or call 911 and describe what you actually see. That is available to you right now and it doesn't require a court.

And you are sitting in a car at night, alone, angry, after a fight, with a form on your phone. That is the worst possible state in which to file a sworn emergency petition. Not because you're a bad person — because it's the state in which people file things they regret. The form will still be there at 9am. Nothing about it expires overnight. If the situation is genuinely an emergency, it will still be one in the morning, and you'll file it with the documents in hand and a judge who takes it seriously.

I'm not going to bless this. Get out of the car and go inside, or go home and sleep. Call the hospice line first if you want to check on him. File in the morning if the documents give you a reason to.

she just texted me saying if i file anything tonight shes telling the hospice to discharge him and hell die alone at home with no care at all isnt that basically a threat shes threatening me shes threatening him and you want me to wait til morning 😩

That text, if it says what you've described, is a serious thing. Telling you she'll have him discharged to punish you for filing is a threat to withdraw care from a dying man to win an argument. That is worth documenting and it is worth acting on — but not by filing the petition tonight, and here's the distinction that matters.

**What that text changes.** It gives you something you didn't have before: a written statement, from the person holding the proxy, that she would use his care as leverage. That's evidence of a motive problem, and it's the first real evidence in this conversation. Save it. Screenshot it, note the time, don't delete it, don't respond in kind.

**What it doesn't change.** It doesn't make tonight the right night to file, and it doesn't make the filing more likely to succeed. Here's why: if she is willing to discharge him to spite you, then a petition she learns about tonight is exactly the trigger she just described. Filing now, at night, on a form you haven't grounded in the documents, hands her the excuse she's threatening to use. You'd be walking into the threat, not defusing it.

**What actually protects him from that threat.** Not a court filing — a phone call. Call the hospice 24-hour line now and tell them, in these words: "I'm the patient's son. The person holding the proxy has told me in writing that she will have him discharged if I take legal action. I'm concerned about his care and I want this on the record." Hospice agencies take that seriously. A discharge for a non-clinical reason, especially one documented as retaliation, is something an agency does not want to be on the wrong side of. That call creates a record with the people who control his care tonight, and it costs you nothing.

**Then, in the morning, with the documents:** if the proxy is invalid, or the certification is defective, or she follows through on the threat, you file — and now you file with her text attached, which is a very different petition than the one you were about to submit an hour ago.

So: no, I'm not telling you to do nothing. I'm telling you the thing to do tonight is the phone call and the screenshot, and the filing is the thing to do in the morning with those two things in hand. The threat is real. The response to it is a record, not a race.
